paper.title: A Recipe for Charge Density Prediction
paper.research_summary: This paper proposes a machine learning method to predict the charge density of atomic systems, aiming to overcome the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in existing approaches. It introduces a recipe combining virtual orbitals, expressive and learnable even-tempered Gaussian basis sets, and a high-capacity equivariant neural network (eSCN) to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy while being more than an order of magnitude faster than prior methods. The method is evaluated on the QM9 charge density benchmark and other datasets.

tasks.objective: To accurately and efficiently predict the charge density of atomic systems (molecules and materials) from their atomic configurations, enabling acceleration of density functional theory calculations.
constraints: scalability for large systems and ab initio molecular dynamics
input_requirements: atomic numbers and coordinates of real atoms
atomic numbers and coordinates of virtual nodes
output_goal: predicted charge density ρ(r) at grid coordinates

evidence.text: In density functional theory, the charge density is the core attribute of atomic systems from which all chemical properties can be derived. Machine learning methods are promising as a means of significantly accelerating charge density predictions, yet existing approaches either lack accuracy or scalability. We propose a recipe that can achieve both.

stages.stage_name_raw: acquisition of DFT-calculated charge density data
stages.stage_goal: To obtain ground-truth charge density data computed via density functional theory for training and evaluation.

evidence.text: The QM9 charge density dataset [18, 19, 7] contains charge density calculations for 133,845 small organic molecules using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP).
We also benchmark our method on the MD charge density dataset [43, 44, 12] and the Cubic charge density dataset [45].

stages.stage_name_raw: construction of atomic and virtual node representations
stages.stage_goal: To prepare input structural representations by placing atomic orbitals at atom centers and virtual orbitals at bond midpoints (for molecules) or void space (for materials), ensuring SE(3)-equivariance.
stage_output: set of virtual nodes (bond midpoints or Voronoi-derived positions)

evidence.text: Due to the critical importance of chemical bonds in defining the overall electronic structure, we insert virtual nodes into the midpoint of all chemical bonds for a given molecule (illustrated in Figure 2 (a)). With this method, the coordinates to insert the virtual nodes are SE(3)-equivariant with regard to the input atom coordinates.
For the materials in the Cubic dataset, we iteratively insert virtual nodes up to the number of atoms in the unit cell using an algorithm based on Voronoi diagrams [55].
evidence.section: Experimental results on MD and Cubic.

stages.stage_name_raw: end-to-end training of equivariant neural network to predict basis coefficients and scaling factors
stages.stage_goal: To train the eSCN-based model to predict orbital basis set coefficients ci,j,m and learnable scaling factors si,j for exponents, minimizing mean-absolute error between predicted and DFT charge densities.
stage_input: coordinates R of real and virtual nodes

evidence.text: Using the atomic orbital basis set representation of charge density, the prediction model aims to predict the basis set coefficients ci,j,m and the scaling factors si,j for each real and virtual node such that the predicted charge density matches the ground truth density obtained from DFT calculations.
We train the model end-to-end with a mean-absolute error loss L over the charge density: L = Er∈Data [|ρ(r) −ˆρ(r)|].

stages.stage_name_raw: benchmarking prediction accuracy and efficiency on test sets
stages.stage_goal: To quantitatively assess model performance using normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) and molecules-per-minute efficiency on held-out test splits.

evidence.text: We benchmark the prediction accuracy with the normalized mean absolute error, defined as: NMAE(ˆρ) = ∫|ρ(r) −ˆρ(r)| dV / ∫|ρ(r)| dV
We benchmark the efficiency of different methods by the number of molecules predicted per minute (Mol. per min.) on a single NVIDIA A100-80GB-PCIe GPU for the QM9 test split.
